chapters.title: Chapter 3: Calculating and Paying Advance Tax

lessons.title: The Instalment Schedule: 15%, 45%, 75% and 100% by the Due Dates

body.text: The advance tax calendar has four dates and one rule: by each date, a cumulative share of your year's tax must be in. Two built-in cushions make the first two dates forgiving, and the last two make no allowances at all. Knowing exactly where those cushions sit is worth more than any tax-saving trick.

children.text: You have already seen the 15%, 45%, 75% and 100% schedule in passing. This lesson treats it properly: what section 408 requires, the tolerance limits hidden in the interest section, what happens when a due date falls on a holiday, and how to plan payments so that none of your instalments ever attracts interest.

markDefs.definition: The 2025 Act section consolidating the presumptive taxation schemes for small businesses, professionals and goods carriage operators (old sections 44AD, 44ADA and 44AE).

children.text: Section 408 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (old section 211) sets the dates. Every taxpayer liable to advance tax follows the same four-date schedule, whether an individual, a firm or a company, unless they declare income under the presumptive scheme in
, in which case the whole amount is due by 15 March.

body.caption: Advance tax schedule for tax year 2026-27
headers: Share of the year's tax paid on this date

body.title: How a year's advance tax is spread across the four dates

children.text: Notice the shape. June asks for only 15%, but September and December each ask for a further 30%, and March for the last 25%. The middle of the year does the heavy lifting, which is exactly when many people least expect a tax bill.

body.title: Quick Check: Cumulative, Not Per Quarter
body.question: Tanya estimates her advance tax for the year at ₹2,40,000. She paid ₹36,000 by 15 June and ₹72,000 more by 15 September. What is the total amount she must have paid by 15 December?
body.explanation: Due dates are cumulative. By 15 December, 75% of ₹2,40,000, which is ₹1,80,000, must have been paid in total. She has paid ₹1,08,000 so far, so her December payment is ₹72,000. ₹72,000 is the December payment, not the cumulative total.

markDefs.definition: The tax on the income you finally declare in your return, less TDS and TCS. Interest for short instalments is measured against this actual figure, not against the estimate you used during the year.

children.text: The interest provision, section 425 (old section 234C), contains a tolerance that many taxpayers never notice. Interest for deferment is measured against your
. For the June and September instalments, no interest applies as long as you have paid at least 12% and 36% respectively. December and March have no cushion.

stats.label: By 15 June
stats.context: Target 15%. Below 12%, interest is charged on the full shortfall from 15% for 3 months

stats.label: By 15 September
stats.context: Target 45%. Below 36%, interest is charged on the full shortfall from 45% for 3 months

stats.label: By 15 December
stats.context: No tolerance. Any shortfall from 75% attracts interest for 3 months

stats.label: By 15 March
stats.context: No tolerance. Any shortfall from 100% attracts interest for 1 month

body.title: Target cumulative percentage and the no-interest floor at each date

children.text: Meghna, an independent HR consultant in Bengaluru, ends the year with tax due on returned income of ₹2,00,000. She paid ₹25,000 by 15 June, which is 12.5%, below the 15% target but above the 12% floor. By 15 September her total was ₹80,000, which is 40%, below 45% but above 36%. She paid ₹1,50,000 in total by 15 December and the full ₹2,00,000 by 15 March. Her interest for deferment is nil.

body.text: The cushion is a floor, not a discount. If you fall below 12% in June, interest is charged on the gap all the way up to 15%, not just up to 12%. The same applies to 36% and 45% in September. Falling just under the floor costs you the entire cushion.

body.title: Try It: The September Floor
body.prompt: Rakesh, a Nagpur-based chartered accountant who keeps regular books, expects tax due on returned income of ₹3,00,000 for the year. What is the minimum cumulative amount he must pay by 15 September to avoid interest for that instalment? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: The September floor is 36% of tax due on returned income. 36% of ₹3,00,000 is ₹1,08,000. The target is 45%, or ₹1,35,000, but paying at least ₹1,08,000 avoids interest for September. He should not rely on the floor for December, though: 75% of ₹3,00,000, ₹2,25,000, must be paid in full by 15 December.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The June Cushion
body.textWithBlank: No interest for deferment is charged on the June instalment if at least ___% of the tax due on returned income has been paid by 15 June.
body.explanation: The June floor is 12%, against a target of 15%. The September floor is 36%, against a target of 45%. There is no floor for December or March.

children.text: All four due dates in tax year 2026-27 fall on weekdays, but that is not true every year. In 2025, for example, 15 June was a Sunday. The long-standing CBDT position, set out in Circular No. 676 of 1994, is that when the last date falls on a day the receiving bank is closed, payment on the next working day is treated as on time, and interest for that instalment is not charged.

body.text: Do not plan around the holiday rule. Interest is computed by a system, and a one-day delay can still show up in an intimation that you then have to contest. With net banking and UPI available on the e-Pay Tax service, the safest habit is to pay by the 10th or 12th of the month. The e-filing portal is notoriously slow on the 14th and 15th of March.

children.text: On Schedule or Paid Up Front?

body.title: Two ways to pay ₹1,00,000 of advance tax

columns.label: Pay exactly on schedule
points: ₹15,000 in June, ₹30,000 in September, ₹30,000 in December, ₹25,000 in March
Money stays in your FD or liquid fund for longer
Needs four reminders and four revisions
Any shortfall in December or March attracts interest immediately

columns.label: Pay the full estimate in June
points: One payment, no further reminders unless income rises
Gives up roughly ₹2,888 of interest at 7% a year on money paid early
If income falls, the excess comes back as a refund with interest of 0.5% a month
Suits people who find the four dates stressful and have spare cash

body.title: Scenario: Suresh's Uneven Year
body.scenario: Suresh runs a small interior fit-out contracting business in Visakhapatnam and keeps regular books. His tax due on returned income for tax year 2026-27 turns out to be ₹4,00,000. Cash flow was lumpy: by 15 June he had paid ₹40,000, by 15 September ₹2,00,000 in total, by 15 December ₹2,40,000 in total, and by 15 March the full ₹4,00,000.
body.prompt: Which instalments attract interest for deferment, and roughly how much? Ignore rounding of amounts, which Chapter 4 covers.
body.modelAnswer: Check each date against its floor. June: he paid 10%, below the 12% floor, so interest applies on the shortfall up to the full 15%. That is ₹60,000 minus ₹40,000, a shortfall of ₹20,000, at 1% a month for 3 months, which is ₹600. September: he had paid 50%, above both the 36% floor and the 45% target, so nil. December: he had paid 60%, and there is no cushion, so the shortfall is ₹3,00,000 minus ₹2,40,000, which is ₹60,000, at 1% a month for 3 months, which is ₹1,800. March: he paid 100%, so nil. Total interest for deferment is about ₹2,400. Paying a slightly larger amount in June (just ₹8,000 more would have reached 12%) and holding back less in December would have avoided all of it.

body.title: Four Reminders That Prevent Interest
steps: Add calendar reminders for 5 June, 5 September, 5 December and 5 March, each labelled with the cumulative percentage due
At each reminder, revise the full-year estimate before calculating the payment
Aim for the full 15% and 45%, and treat 12% and 36% only as a safety net
Treat 75% by 15 December and 100% by 15 March as hard deadlines with no cushion
Pay by the 10th to avoid last-minute portal and bank delays, and download every challan receipt
If you use presumptive taxation, set one firm reminder for early March, and consider paying some earlier anyway

cards.definition: Sets the advance tax due dates: 15%, 45%, 75% and 100% cumulatively by 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March.
Charges simple interest of 1% a month on instalment shortfalls: 3 months for June, September and December, 1 month for March.
No interest for June if at least 12% of tax due on returned income is paid by 15 June.
No interest for September if at least 36% is paid by 15 September.
Tax on the income finally declared in the return, less TDS and TCS. Instalment shortfalls are measured against this, not your estimate.
Under CBDT Circular No. 676, if the due date falls on a day the bank is closed, payment on the next working day is treated as on time.

points: Advance tax is due cumulatively: 15% by 15 June, 45% by 15 September, 75% by 15 December and 100% by 15 March
September and December each carry 30% of the year's tax, making them the heaviest instalments
No interest applies for June if at least 12% is paid, or for September if at least 36% is paid; December and March have no cushion
Falling below a floor means interest on the full gap up to 15% or 45%, not just up to the floor
Shortfalls are measured against tax due on the income you finally return, so underestimates catch up with you
Pay a few days early rather than relying on the holiday rule or a working portal on the 15th

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax, legal or investment advice. Section references are to the Income-tax Act, 2025, with the corresponding Income-tax Act, 1961 section in brackets. Interest figures are simplified and ignore rounding rules covered in Chapter 4. Dates, percentages and circulars reflect the position understood at the time of writing. Verify current rules or consult a qualified chartered accountant before acting.
